papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: The Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD can transfer output behavior, intermediate representations, and structural properties from teachers to students. A rich family of methods—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, multi-teacher strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—demonstrate that KD is not a single technique but a design space. The effectiveness of KD depends on factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the nature and complexity of data, task specificity, and availability of unlabeled data; these trade-offs motivate hybrid strategies that combine representation-focused distillation, curriculum-like teacher schedules, and structured pruning to maximize both accuracy and inference efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and How to Use It
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and flexible route to producing compact, high-performance models for deep learning and NLP. When matched to task requirements and student capacity and when combined with complementary compression strategies, distillation routinely yields models that approach the accuracy of large teachers while delivering meaningful latency and memory gains. However, distillation is not universally superior: its benefits depend on what form of knowledge is transferred, the availability and complexity of training data, and the desired properties (e.g., robustness, latency). I argue that distillation should be treated as an indispensable component of a compression toolbox — applied with representation-level signals, teacher-aware adaptations, and hybridization with pruning or progressive replacement when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains the most flexible and broadly applicable approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD is best treated as a toolbox: different distillation signals (logits, hidden states, attention/feature correlations), teacher schedules (offline, online/evolutionary, multi-teacher selection), and complementary techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, robustness objectives) should be chosen and combined according to task requirements, student capacity, data availability, and latency or robustness constraints. When KD is designed to align transferred information with student capacity and task needs it yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, NLP, generation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD delivers consistent gains when its objectives and signals (logits, internal representations, attention maps, contrastive or adversarial losses) are matched to student capacity and task constraints and when it is combined with complementary compression strategies such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. However, KD is not universally optimal: careful teacher design, task-aware signal selection, and hybrid pipelines are often required to realize the best latency–accuracy–robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: A Distillation-First Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single recipe. Best results arise from (1) transferring internal, structured representations in addition to logits, (2) adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and (3) combining distillation with complementary compression strategies such as progressive module replacement or structured pruning. This position synthesizes empirical and algorithmic advances to recommend practical design patterns for building compact, robust models for deployment in vision, language, and reinforcement-learning settings.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce compact models that retain much of the performance of large networks by transferring knowledge from one or more teacher models to a student. Research over the last decade has diversified the KD toolkit beyond soft-label supervision to include internal representation matching, adversarial objectives, contrastive and Wasserstein distances, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schemes, teacher-training strategies, and task-aware filter selection. These approaches have been applied across computer vision, NLP (including pretrained Transformers and summarization), retrieval, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Practical trade-offs arise from teacher-student capacity gaps, data requirements, optimization difficulties, and robustness concerns; contemporary work addresses these by narrowing capability gaps (e.g., evolving or student-friendly teachers), selecting or weighting teacher signals, and distilling only task-relevant intermediate features. Empirical studies show that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: the best choice depends on model architectures, target tasks, and constraints on data, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that success depends less on a single canonical loss and more on how teacher knowledge is selected, represented, and adapted to the student and the target task. Best results arise when distillation methods (1) expose informative internal representations rather than only final logits, (2) adapt or curate teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and (3) combine distillation with complementary compression strategies (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement). When applied with attention to these aspects, distillation yields compact models that maintain high accuracy, can inherit robustness, and scale to practical inference budgets.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and representational structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. KD has evolved from simple soft-label matching into a configurable toolbox that includes logits matching, intermediate-representation alignment, attention and feature-correlation transfer, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and multi- or online-teacher schedules. When matched to student capacity, task demands, and data availability—and when combined thoughtfully with complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement—KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency and resource constraints. However, its effectiveness depends on the form of transferred signals, teacher–student gaps, and robustness or data limitations, motivating hybrid, task-aware designs and continued research into teacher adaptation and training schedules.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring outputs, internal representations, and training dynamics from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, task-aware layer-wise filtering, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and analytical work across vision and NLP shows that distillation, when matched to student capacity and task constraints and often combined with complementary compression methods, reliably improves compact-model performance while exposing remaining challenges in robustness, data requirements, and teacher–student mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Toolbox: Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategies for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students, but its success hinges on matching the distillation strategy to task demands, student capacity, and data constraints. Rather than a single recipe, KD should be treated as a flexible toolbox combining soft-labels, internal-representation alignment, teacher adaptation, layer-wise filtering, adversarial objectives, and pruning or module-replacement where appropriate. When chosen and combined thoughtfully—exposing informative internal signals, adapting teacher supervision to student capacity, and using task-aware selection—KD yields compact models that retain high performance, robustness, and practical latency gains.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. When designed to match what is transferred (logits, internal representations, attention or feature correlations) and how teachers and students are coupled (teacher engineering, online or multi-teacher schemes, curriculum or route-based schedules), KD routinely produces compact models that approach the performance of large teachers while meeting real-world latency, memory, and robustness requirements. The most reliable practice combines representation-focused distillation with teacher adaptation and, when necessary, complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement to address severe latency or data constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models or produce compact subnetworks via pruning and module replacement. The literature has grown into a design space of methods that transfer final outputs (soft logits), internal representations (feature maps, attention, layer activations), or training dynamics (curricula, evolving teachers), and which operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive-replacement regimes. Empirical and analytical work shows that success depends on matching the distilled information to student capacity and task demands, combining complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning or module replacement) when appropriate, and addressing practical constraints such as unlabeled-data needs, robustness transfer, and optimization stability. Effective distillation usually involves exposing informative internal signals, adapting teacher supervision to the student, and selecting task-relevant knowledge rather than naively copying all teacher behavior.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, effective distillation is a design space of complementary techniques — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi- or evolving-teacher schedules, student-friendly teacher design, and hybrid pipelines that combine pruning or progressive module replacement. When chosen and combined with attention to teacher–student capacity, task characteristics, and data availability, distillation reliably yields compact models that preserve accuracy and can transfer robustness; when misapplied it can be outperformed by simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or structured pruning strategies. I argue that the best practical posture is to treat distillation as a task-aware hybrid toolbox: prioritize representation-level transfer and teacher engineering, use confidence- or task-aware weighting for multiple signals, integrate robustness-aware objectives when needed, and combine distillation with pruning or module replacement when latency/memory constraints dominate.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Distilling Dense Representations for Ranking using Tightly-Coupled Teachers
papers_seen.abstract: We present an approach to ranking with dense representations that applies knowledge distillation to improve the recently proposed late-interaction ColBERT model. Specifically, we distill the knowledge from ColBERT's expressive MaxSim operator for computing relevance scores into a simple dot product, thus enabling single-step ANN search. Our key insight is that during distillation, tight coupling between the teacher model and the student model enables more flexible distillation strategies and yields better learned representations. We empirically show that our approach improves query latency and greatly reduces the onerous storage requirements of ColBERT, while only making modest sacrifices in terms of effectiveness. By combining our dense representations with sparse representations derived from document expansion, we are able to approach the effectiveness of a standard cross-encoder reranker using BERT that is orders of magnitude slower.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Its effectiveness stems from several complementary mechanisms—soft-target supervision, alignment of intermediate representations, and shaping of training dynamics—and from its flexibility to be combined with methods such as progressive module replacement and structured pruning. While distillation often delivers strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, realizing those gains requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to adapt the teacher signal to student capacity, and when to hybridize distillation with other compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably improves inference speed and memory footprint while often preserving accuracy, but its success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity and task needs. Best outcomes come from hybrid, task-aware pipelines that combine representation-level distillation, teacher adaptation or selection, and complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) to address data, latency, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Work across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding shows KD variants — from soft-label matching to internal-representation alignment, teacher adaptation, adversarial and curriculum-based schedules, and hybrid pipelines combining pruning or module replacement — routinely recover much of teacher performance when the distillation strategy is matched to task demands and student capacity. Important limitations remain: sensitivity to teacher–student capacity gaps, reliance on unlabeled data and heavy distillation compute in some pipelines, and uneven transfer of robustness, motivating continued research into targeted transfer signals and efficient, student-aware distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible set of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to achieve deployable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Rather than a single recipe, KD comprises response-based, representation-based, adversarial, and meta- or multi-teacher methods that should be chosen and combined according to student capacity, task demands, and available data. When designed with task-aware choices of transferred signals and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance; however, success requires careful management of teacher–student mismatch, data requirements, and robustness transfer.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Research converges on three core ideas: (1) the form of transferred information matters (from soft logits to internal representations and inter-feature statistics), (2) the teacher–student relationship and training schedule should be adapted to the student capacity and task, and (3) hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, curriculum or adversarial objectives, and task-aware filtering yield the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Empirical work across machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, non-autoregressive generation, vision, and 3D detection demonstrates large gains but also exposes sensitivity to data complexity, teacher selection, and capacity gaps, motivating ongoing research into targeted transfer mechanisms and efficient distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central and Complementary Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical, versatile, and central approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones across vision and NLP. KD can transfer outputs, internal representations, and structure from teacher to student, and—when combined with task-aware selection, adaptive teacher schedules, or structured pruning—yields strong trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. However, KD has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute requirements, and potential optimization mismatches; these limits motivate hybrid pipelines and careful design choices that match what is distilled to the student’s capacity and the target application.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger models to smaller ones to improve efficiency while preserving or enhancing performance. Research has explored why distillation works, how to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information), and how to adapt distillation to settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, continual/incremental learning, task-specific compression, and robustness. A rich set of algorithmic families has emerged — including layer-wise and module-replacement schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher-student co-training and evolution, pruning combined with distillation, and task-aware filtering — each addressing capacity gaps, representation mismatch, or computational constraints in different ways. Empirical studies across vision, NLP (including machine translation, summarization, and dense retrieval), reinforcement learning, and 3D detection demonstrate both substantial gains and important failure modes, motivating continued work on matching distilled information to student capacity and task requirements.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Methods span soft-label (logit) matching, alignment of intermediate representations and attention maps, teacher design strategies (offline, online, multi- or evolving teachers), adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum or confidence-weighted schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective application requires matching what is distilled to the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals to task constraints and data availability, and often combining distillation with complementary compression methods to meet latency, robustness, and data-budget goals.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Pre-trained Summarization Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent state-of-the-art approaches to summarization utilize large pre-trained Transformer models. Distilling these models to smaller student models has become critically important for practical use; however there are many different distillation methods proposed by the NLP literature. Recent work on distilling BERT for classification and regression tasks shows strong performance using direct knowledge distillation. Alternatively, machine translation practitioners distill using pseudo-labeling, where a small model is trained on the translations of a larger model. A third, simpler approach is to 'shrink and fine-tune' (SFT), which avoids any explicit distillation by copying parameters to a smaller student model and then fine-tuning. We compare these three approaches for distillation of Pegasus and BART, the current and former state of the art, pre-trained summarization models, and find that SFT outperforms knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, but under-performs pseudo-labeling on the more abstractive XSUM dataset. PyTorch Code and checkpoints of different sizes are available through Hugging Face transformers here http://tiny.cc/4iy0tz.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. By selecting and combining appropriate distilled signals (soft labels, intermediate representations, attention/feature statistics), adapting or engineering teachers to student capacity, and integrating complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum schedules), practitioners can produce compact models that retain high accuracy and practical latency. Success requires matching what is transferred to the student and the task, using multi- or evolving-teacher schemes where helpful, and guarding against mismatches or unnecessary constraints imposed by poorly chosen teacher signals.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central, versatile technique for producing compact, high-performing models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD succeeds by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and structured behaviors from teachers to students, but no single KD recipe dominates all settings. The most reliable practical approach is hybrid and task-aware: expose informative internal representations, adapt teacher signals to student capacity and the target task, and combine distillation with complementary compression methods such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or targeted robustness procedures to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. The literature shows many complementary algorithmic families — soft-target (logit) transfer, internal-representation and attention/feature matching, contrastive and adversarial objectives, progressive module replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical work across vision, NLP, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning indicates that no single recipe dominates: careful matching of what is distilled to student capacity and task needs, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods tend to give the best accuracy–latency–size trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, hidden states, feature correlations, decision-boundary information), how teachers are chosen or adapted, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression methods, distillation routinely yields compact models that preserve much of the accuracy of larger models while meeting latency and memory constraints. However, KD is not a single recipe: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity gaps, task characteristics, data availability, and robustness requirements, which motivate task-aware, teacher-aware, and hybrid distillation practices.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: The Continuing Value of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP (and When Hybrids Are Better)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students for deployment in resource-constrained environments. KD works through multiple mechanisms — smoothing/regularization, transfer of structured class- and instance-level information, and alignment of internal representations — and can be improved by task-aware, teacher-aware, and curriculum-inspired strategies. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all solution: structured pruning and module-replacement methods can match or exceed KD under certain data- or compute-constrained regimes, and simple strategies like shrink-and-fine-tune sometimes outperform explicit distillation for particular pre-trained NLP models and datasets. Best outcomes typically come from principled combinations: selecting or training student-friendly teachers, matching intermediate representations selectively, using task-aware filters, and combining KD with pruning or specialized distillation objectives tailored to the model and task.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and its Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning based models are relatively large, and it is hard to deploy such models on resource-limited devices such as mobile phones and embedded devices. One possible solution is knowledge distillation whereby a smaller model (student model) is trained by utilizing the information from a larger model (teacher model). In this paper, we present a survey of knowledge distillation techniques applied to deep learning models. To compare the performances of different techniques, we propose a new metric called distillation metric. Distillation metric compares different knowledge distillation algorithms based on sizes and accuracy scores. Based on the survey, some interesting conclusions are drawn and presented in this paper.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably improves inference speed and memory footprint while often preserving accuracy, but its success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity and task needs. Best outcomes come from hybrid, task-aware pipelines that combine representation-level distillation, teacher adaptation or selection, and complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) to address data, latency, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Pre-trained Summarization Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent state-of-the-art approaches to summarization utilize large pre-trained Transformer models. Distilling these models to smaller student models has become critically important for practical use; however there are many different distillation methods proposed by the NLP literature. Recent work on distilling BERT for classification and regression tasks shows strong performance using direct knowledge distillation. Alternatively, machine translation practitioners distill using pseudo-labeling, where a small model is trained on the translations of a larger model. A third, simpler approach is to 'shrink and fine-tune' (SFT), which avoids any explicit distillation by copying parameters to a smaller student model and then fine-tuning. We compare these three approaches for distillation of Pegasus and BART, the current and former state of the art, pre-trained summarization models, and find that SFT outperforms knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, but under-performs pseudo-labeling on the more abstractive XSUM dataset. papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central, versatile technique for producing compact, high-performing models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD succeeds by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and structured behaviors from teachers to students, but no single KD recipe dominates all settings. The most reliable practical approach is hybrid and task-aware: expose informative internal representations, adapt teacher signals to student capacity and the target task, and combine distillation with complementary compression methods such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or targeted robustness procedures to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. By selecting what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or structured behaviors), adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or teacher adaptation), practitioners can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Effective compression requires matching distillation strategies to task demands, data availability, and deployment constraints; blindly applying a single distillation recipe risks wasted effort or suboptimal trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates predictive behavior from large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster models for deployment under resource constraints. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a broad toolbox that includes intermediate-representation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and evolutionary teachers, confidence-weighted and task-aware strategies, and integrations with pruning or module-replacement. Across vision and NLP tasks these methods enable substantial reductions in parameters and latency while often retaining a large fraction of teacher performance, though success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity, selecting or adapting teachers, and addressing data and robustness constraints. Practical best practice is to select and combine KD variants according to task demands and resource constraints rather than rely on a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware design space that can reliably compress large models into smaller, deployable students when its signals and schedules are matched to student capacity and task constraints. Combining soft-target transfer with representation-level alignment, teacher engineering (including multi- and online-teacher schemes and meta-learned teachers), adversarial/contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that integrate pruning or progressive module replacement produces the strongest empirical trade-offs in latency, memory, and accuracy. Important caveats remain — notably teacher–student capacity gaps, data-complexity effects, and imperfect robustness transfer — which motivate careful choice of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: The Role of Knowledge Distillation in Compressing Deep and NLP Models: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable models. It works through multiple mechanisms — soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, and structured guidance — and can be adapted via curriculum strategies, multi-teacher weighting, adversarial or decision-boundary-aware examples, and progressive module replacement. Distillation often yields models that approach teacher accuracy while improving latency and memory, but its success depends on matching distillation methods to task properties and model capacity; in some settings structured pruning or hybrid approaches can match or exceed distillation without the need for large unlabeled corpora. I argue that distillation is indispensable for practical NLP and deep learning deployments when used with task-aware, representation-level, and teacher-aware strategies, and that combining distillation with complementary compression methods yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. By selecting and combining appropriate distilled signals (soft labels, intermediate representations, attention/feature statistics), adapting or engineering teachers to student capacity, and integrating complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum schedules), practitioners can produce compact models that retain high accuracy and practical latency. Success requires matching what is transferred to the student and the task, using multi- or evolving-teacher schemes where helpful, and guarding against mismatches or unnecessary constraints imposed by poorly chosen teacher signals.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices (Synthesis)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for producing compact, deployable deep models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students. Over the last decade KD diversified from simple soft-label transfer into many variants that match logits, internal representations, attention/feature maps, or training dynamics, and that interact with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning and progressive module replacement. Practical deployment benefits most from hybrid, task-aware strategies that select what to transfer, adapt the teacher-student relationship, and combine distillation with pruning or architectural replacement to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is best understood not as a single recipe but as a configurable, hybrid toolbox for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Effective compression designs expose and transfer informative internal signals (not only logits), adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combine distillation with complementary techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum strategies) when latency, memory, or robustness requirements demand it. Practical deployment requires choosing what to transfer and how to manage teacher–student dynamics, sometimes preferring simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or pruning-first strategies under tight data or compute constraints.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolkit for producing compact models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD improves student performance by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and training dynamics, but its success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, task demands, and deployment constraints. Best practice treats KD as part of a hybrid compression pipeline—selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement when needed.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. The literature shows KD is not a single recipe but a design space of techniques (logits, internal representations, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules) that, when matched to student capacity and task demands and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), yield strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective practice requires selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to the student, and hybridizing distillation with pruning or architecture-aware replacement where appropriate; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible family of techniques for transferring the behavior and internal structure of large models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from soft-label matching into a broad design space that includes logits transfer, layer- and feature-wise alignment, attention or correlation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and progressive module replacement. Practical success is task- and capacity-aware: practitioners must choose what to transfer, adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and often combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, module replacement, or shrink-and-fine-tune) to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints. While KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance in many vision and NLP tasks, its effectiveness depends on data complexity, teacher–student gaps, and the choice of transferred signals, and alternative or hybrid pipelines can be preferable in some regimes.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible set of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to achieve deployable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Rather than a single recipe, KD comprises response-based, representation-based, adversarial, and meta- or multi-teacher methods that should be chosen and combined according to student capacity, task demands, and available data. When designed with task-aware choices of transferred signals and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance; however, success requires careful management of teacher–student mismatch, data requirements, and robustness transfer.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Its strengths arise from multiple complementary mechanisms (soft targets, internal representation transfer, teacher engineering, and supervised schedules), and the most reliable practical strategies treat KD as a configurable toolbox that is combined with pruning or module replacement when deployment constraints demand it. Practitioners obtain the best trade-offs by matching distilled signals to student capacity, adapting teacher dynamics to the task, and using hybrid pipelines tailored to data, latency, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Indispensable Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware design space rather than a single algorithm. By transferring behavioral and representational signals from larger teachers to smaller students, KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost. When carefully matched to student capacity and task constraints — and when combined with complementary techniques such as pruning, confidence weighting, and targeted representation transfer — KD yields practical, deployable models with strong accuracy–latency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox of methods for producing compact, deployable models. Contemporary KD techniques include matching logits, aligning internal representations or attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student capacity gaps, task complexity, and data availability. Practical compression typically requires selecting or adapting distilled signals to student capacity and combining complementary methods to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the last decade KD has expanded from soft-target matching into a rich toolkit that includes internal-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred information to student capacity and task constraints, and on making teacher signals student-friendly. KD is therefore best used as a task-aware toolbox rather than a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a broadly useful and adaptable family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP, KD methods extend beyond soft-target matching to include internal-representation transfer, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how it is transferred to student capacity, task properties, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: On Learning the Geodesic Path for Incremental Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Neural networks notoriously suffer from the problem of catastrophic forgetting, the phenomenon of forgetting the past knowledge when acquiring new knowledge. Overcoming catastrophic forgetting is of significant importance to emulate the process of "incremental learning", where the model is capable of learning from sequential experience in an efficient and robust way. State-of-the-art techniques for incremental learning make use of knowledge distillation towards preventing catastrophic forgetting. Therein, one updates the network while ensuring that the network's responses to previously seen concepts remain stable throughout updates. This in practice is done by minimizing the dissimilarity between current and previous responses of the network one way or another. Our work contributes a novel method to the arsenal of distillation techniques. In contrast to the previous state of the art, we propose to firstly construct low-dimensional manifolds for previous and current responses and minimize the dissimilarity between the responses along the geodesic connecting the manifolds. This induces a more formidable knowledge distillation with smooth properties which preserves the past knowledge more efficiently as observed by our comprehensive empirical study.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and representational structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. KD has evolved from simple soft-label matching into a configurable toolbox that includes logits matching, intermediate-representation alignment, attention and feature-correlation transfer, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and multi- or online-teacher schedules. When matched to student capacity, task demands, and data availability—and when combined thoughtfully with complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement—KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency and resource constraints. However, its effectiveness depends on the form of transferred signals, teacher–student gaps, and robustness or data limitations, motivating hybrid, task-aware designs and continued research into teacher adaptation and training schedules.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models in deep learning and NLP. Its power arises from multiple distinct mechanisms of transfer (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, and training dynamics) and from the flexibility to combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, adversarial objectives, and curriculum schedules). KD is not a universal panacea: its success depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity, adapting teacher signals over training, and considering data, latency, and robustness constraints. Best practice treats KD as a hybrid, task-aware toolbox whose components are chosen and combined to meet the target application’s constraints and goals.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD's strength derives from a flexible design space — transferring logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations, and decision-boundary information — and from compatibility with complementary strategies such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, and teacher adaptation. While KD does not universally dominate every setting, when applied in a task-aware, representation-focused, and teacher-aware way it reliably yields compact models that approach teacher performance while delivering practical latency, memory, and robustness benefits.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central and Complementary Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a versatile and effective approach for compressing large models into compact, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD’s strengths arise from its ability to transfer soft targets, internal representations, and task-relevant signals to reshape student training dynamics, and it admits many practical variants (multi-teacher, adversarial, curriculum, online/evolutionary, and progressive replacement). At the same time, structured pruning and module-replacement methods can be competitive or complementary when latency, data, or compute constraints dominate. Best practice is a toolbox mentality: choose what to transfer to match student capacity, adapt the teacher–student relationship during training, and combine distillation with pruning or curriculum strategies when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware design space that can reliably compress large models into smaller, deployable students when its signals and schedules are matched to student capacity and task constraints. Combining soft-target transfer with representation-level alignment, teacher engineering (including multi- and online-teacher schemes and meta-learned teachers), adversarial/contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that integrate pruning or progressive module replacement produces the strongest empirical trade-offs in latency, memory, and accuracy. Important caveats remain — notably teacher–student capacity gaps, data-complexity effects, and imperfect robustness transfer — which motivate careful choice of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models by transferring information from a teacher to a smaller student. Methods vary widely: matching output soft-labels, aligning intermediate representations, adversarial and contrastive approaches, curriculum and meta-learning strategies, and task-aware layer selection. In NLP, and particularly with large pretrained Transformers, distillation is applied both during pretraining and fine-tuning; alternative compression strategies (e.g., pruning) are often combined with distillation to trade off size, speed, and accuracy. Empirical and theoretical work highlights multiple mechanisms by which distillation helps students, including regularization, reduced data complexity, and per-instance gradient shaping.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used family of techniques that compress large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. KD has evolved from soft-label matching into many variants—intermediate-representation alignment, contrastive and adversarial objectives, curriculum and route-based supervision, online/multi-teacher strategies, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the type of transferred signal to student capacity and task demands, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques to meet latency, memory, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Its strengths arise from multiple complementary mechanisms (soft targets, internal representation transfer, teacher engineering, and supervised schedules), and the most reliable practical strategies treat KD as a configurable toolbox that is combined with pruning or module replacement when deployment constraints demand it. Practitioners obtain the best trade-offs by matching distilled signals to student capacity, adapting teacher dynamics to the task, and using hybrid pipelines tailored to data, latency, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD's strength derives from a flexible design space — transferring logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations, and decision-boundary information — and from compatibility with complementary strategies such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, and teacher adaptation. While KD does not universally dominate every setting, when applied in a task-aware, representation-focused, and teacher-aware way it reliably yields compact models that approach teacher performance while delivering practical latency, memory, and robustness benefits.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students. Research over the past decade has expanded KD from simple soft-target matching into a wide set of techniques that transfer final outputs, intermediate representations, attention and feature correlations, and decision-boundary information. Practical success depends on choosing which signals to transfer, adapting teacher behavior to student capacity and task constraints, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (e.g., pruning or progressive module replacement) when latency, memory, or robustness demands require hybrid solutions. Despite strong empirical gains across vision and NLP, open challenges remain in reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student capacity gaps and data requirements.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. The literature shows KD is not a single recipe but a design space of techniques (logits, internal representations, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules) that, when matched to student capacity and task demands and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), yield strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective practice requires selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to the student, and hybridizing distillation with pruning or architecture-aware replacement where appropriate; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods form a broad, task-aware toolbox for turning large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students. The literature spans soft-target (logit) matching, alignment of internal representations and attention, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically requires adapting teacher signals to student capacity, selecting which signals to transfer given task constraints, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a configurable, task-aware toolbox — selecting which signals to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and hybridizing distillation with complementary compression methods — KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. However, KD has limits (data and teacher–student mismatch, compute cost) and should be compared against or combined with pruning and simple baselines in constrained regimes.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models by transferring useful predictive behavior and internal structure from teacher models to smaller students. The field encompasses a wide spectrum of techniques — matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, layer-wise or module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher strategies, and combinations with structured pruning — each suited to different capacity gaps, data regimes, latency constraints, and robustness needs. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation helps by smoothing supervision, reducing data complexity, shaping per-instance gradients and decision boundaries, and providing representational priors that smaller models can exploit. Effective compression typically requires choosing or adapting what is transferred to the student's capacity and the target task, and often benefits from hybrid strategies (e.g., distillation plus pruning or progressive replacement).

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones across vision and NLP. The literature provides many complementary distillation objectives and workflows — soft-label transfer, intermediate-representation matching, adversarial/contrastive losses, online and multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effectiveness depends strongly on teacher–student capacity gaps, the exact form of transferred information, task characteristics, and data availability; best practice is to select or adapt distillation signals to the student and downstream task and to combine methods where appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible set of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with task awareness — selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques — distillation routinely yields compact models that recover much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Practical success depends on careful design choices (what to match, how to adapt teachers, and whether to incorporate pruning or progressive replacement) rather than a single canonical recipe.

Extensive experiments on two vision tasks, includ-ing ImageNet classification and Pascal VOC segmentation,demonstrate the superiority of our ICKD, which consis-tently outperforms many existing methods, advancing thestate-of-the-art in the fields of Knowledge Distillation.
