papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably improves inference speed and memory footprint while often preserving accuracy, but its success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity and task needs. Best outcomes come from hybrid, task-aware pipelines that combine representation-level distillation, teacher adaptation or selection, and complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) to address data, latency, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster ones by transferring useful information from teacher models to students. Methods span matching teacher output distributions (soft labels), aligning internal representations at various granularities, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware or curriculum-based strategies. Distillation is used both for deployment-efficient models and as a tool in related problems (e.g., continual learning, pruning, robustness, retrieval, and task transfer). Empirical and theoretical work shows that what is transferred (e.g., global/class relations, instance-level difficulty signals, intermediate features) and how it is transferred (e.g., offline vs online, multi-teacher weighting, attention/feature matching, adversarial objectives) critically affect student performance. Practical trade-offs include compute and data requirements, robustness transfer, and the relative roles of pruning and distillation; newer work emphasizes making teacher signals more student-friendly and selecting or filtering teacher knowledge to match student capacity and the downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring outputs, internal representations, and training dynamics from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, task-aware layer-wise filtering, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and analytical work across vision and NLP shows that distillation, when matched to student capacity and task constraints and often combined with complementary compression methods, reliably improves compact-model performance while exposing remaining challenges in robustness, data requirements, and teacher–student mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains the most flexible and broadly applicable approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD is best treated as a toolbox: different distillation signals (logits, hidden states, attention/feature correlations), teacher schedules (offline, online/evolutionary, multi-teacher selection), and complementary techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, robustness objectives) should be chosen and combined according to task requirements, student capacity, data availability, and latency or robustness constraints. When KD is designed to align transferred information with student capacity and task needs it yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, NLP, generation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques provide a flexible design space for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students. Methods include soft-target (logit) matching, internal-representation alignment, layer- or module-wise replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, confidence- or curriculum-weighted supervision, and adversarial or contrastive objectives. Empirical results across vision and NLP show that combining representation-level transfer with teacher engineering and complementary compression (pruning or progressive replacement) typically yields the best trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and model size. Success depends on matching what is distilled to student capacity, adapting teacher signals to task constraints, and accounting for data complexity and robustness needs.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the last decade KD has expanded from soft-target matching into a rich toolkit that includes internal-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred information to student capacity and task constraints, and on making teacher signals student-friendly. KD is therefore best used as a task-aware toolbox rather than a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and flexible family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. The literature treats KD as a design space rather than a single recipe: practitioners transfer soft logits, internal representations, attention/feature statistics, or training dynamics; they use offline, online/evolving, multi-teacher, or self-distillation schedules; and they often combine KD with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective distillation aligns the form and amount of transferred information with student capacity and task needs, and best practice is task-aware, hybrid, and selective about what to copy from the teacher.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates predictive behavior from large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster models for deployment under resource constraints. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a broad toolbox that includes intermediate-representation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and evolutionary teachers, confidence-weighted and task-aware strategies, and integrations with pruning or module-replacement. Across vision and NLP tasks these methods enable substantial reductions in parameters and latency while often retaining a large fraction of teacher performance, though success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity, selecting or adapting teachers, and addressing data and robustness constraints. Practical best practice is to select and combine KD variants according to task demands and resource constraints rather than rely on a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher. The literature expands beyond simple soft-label matching to include internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filters, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, meta-learned teachers, and complementary pruning strategies. Applications span NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive translation, summarization, dense retrieval), vision (classification, detection, pose regression), reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Key practical concerns include the teacher–student capacity gap, selection or weighting of teacher signals, reliance on unlabeled data, robustness, and efficient architectural shrinking. Empirical and theoretical work characterizes what is transferred (from label-smoothing-like regularization to instance-specific gradient rescaling and internal concept representations) and proposes methods to better align student representations with useful teacher knowledge. Open directions include task-aware selection of representational targets, minimizing unnecessary constraints from converged teachers, and combining structured pruning with targeted distillation to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques aim to transfer useful predictive behavior and internal structure from larger, expensive models to smaller, faster models. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, feature distributions, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are coupled (offline, online, multi-teacher, evolutionary, or self-distillation), and what additional objectives or defenses are used (adversarial training, contrastive losses, curriculum-based routing, or geodesic alignment). Distillation has been applied broadly across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding, and interacts with pruning and other compression strategies. Practical trade-offs include the teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness, and the form of supervision needed for good transfer.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Mechanisms, Variants, Task Considerations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring useful information from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple soft-target matching into a rich set of methods that transfer logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information; use single, multiple, evolving, or learned teachers; and combine with pruning or module replacement. Practical success depends on aligning what is transferred to student capacity and task requirements, and best results typically come from hybrid, task-aware strategies that match distillation signals to model and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large pretrained models into smaller, more efficient models by transferring learned knowledge from teacher to student. A rich variety of techniques have been developed: matching soft targets, aligning intermediate and internal representations, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based supervision, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, self-distillation, and hybrid approaches that combine pruning with distillation. These techniques have been applied across vision, language, retrieval, and reinforcement learning tasks, and have been analyzed to explain when and why distillation helps. Empirical work shows distillation can reduce model size and preserve or improve performance, but effectiveness depends on the choice of teacher, the form of transferred knowledge, data complexity, and task-specific design choices.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. The literature shows KD is not a single recipe but a design space of techniques (logits, internal representations, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules) that, when matched to student capacity and task demands and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), yield strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective practice requires selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to the student, and hybridizing distillation with pruning or architecture-aware replacement where appropriate; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practically central approach for producing compact neural models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. Research over the past decade has expanded KD from simple soft-label matching to a diverse toolkit that includes internal-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schedules, student-friendly teacher training, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals and teacher strategies to student capacity, task requirements, and available data; when designed carefully, KD enables substantial latency and memory gains while retaining strong accuracy across vision, NLP, ranking, retrieval, and reinforcement-learning tasks.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Remains Central for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Principles, Variants, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a simple teacher-to-student soft-label transfer into a rich family of methods that target robustness, internal representation alignment, task-specific selection of signals, and efficient compression pipelines. Across vision, language, and sequence generation tasks, distillation enables compact models to retain or approach the performance of large models while enabling practical latency and memory benefits. Effective distillation designs combine multiple signals (logits, hidden states, feature correlations), adapt the teacher-student relationship during training, and can be integrated with pruning or module-replacement strategies to achieve strong trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has broadened from soft-label matching to include representation-level transfer, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Its effectiveness depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combining complementary compression techniques when data, latency, or robustness demands require it. Best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox rather than a single recipe.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger models to smaller ones to improve efficiency while preserving or enhancing performance. Research has explored why distillation works, how to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information), and how to adapt distillation to settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, continual/incremental learning, task-specific compression, and robustness. A rich set of algorithmic families has emerged — including layer-wise and module-replacement schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher-student co-training and evolution, pruning combined with distillation, and task-aware filtering — each addressing capacity gaps, representation mismatch, or computational constraints in different ways. Empirical studies across vision, NLP (including machine translation, summarization, and dense retrieval), reinforcement learning, and 3D detection demonstrate both substantial gains and important failure modes, motivating continued work on matching distilled information to student capacity and task requirements.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: The Role of Knowledge Distillation in Compressing Deep and NLP Models: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable models. It works through multiple mechanisms — soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, and structured guidance — and can be adapted via curriculum strategies, multi-teacher weighting, adversarial or decision-boundary-aware examples, and progressive module replacement. Distillation often yields models that approach teacher accuracy while improving latency and memory, but its success depends on matching distillation methods to task properties and model capacity; in some settings structured pruning or hybrid approaches can match or exceed distillation without the need for large unlabeled corpora. I argue that distillation is indispensable for practical NLP and deep learning deployments when used with task-aware, representation-level, and teacher-aware strategies, and that combining distillation with complementary compression methods yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer useful predictive behavior from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students) while preserving accuracy and often adding desirable properties such as robustness or task-specific efficiency. A wide range of methods has been developed: soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer- or module-wise compression, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, and hybrid approaches that combine pruning with distillation. Empirical results across vision, language, ranking, summarization, and reinforcement learning show that carefully chosen distillation strategies can reclaim much of a teacher's performance in a compact student, but outcomes depend strongly on the choice of distilled signals, the alignment of capacities, teacher selection or adaptation, and task-specific constraints. Recent work also emphasizes robustness transfer, task-aware filtering of teacher signals, and alternatives to distillation such as structured pruning that can match distillation in latency without extra unlabeled data. Remaining challenges include principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer, scaling to diverse prediction tasks, and combining distillation with compression and robustness objectives in a computationally efficient way.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models by transferring useful predictive behavior and internal structure from teacher models to smaller students. The field encompasses a wide spectrum of techniques — matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, layer-wise or module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher strategies, and combinations with structured pruning — each suited to different capacity gaps, data regimes, latency constraints, and robustness needs. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation helps by smoothing supervision, reducing data complexity, shaping per-instance gradients and decision boundaries, and providing representational priors that smaller models can exploit. Effective compression typically requires choosing or adapting what is transferred to the student's capacity and the target task, and often benefits from hybrid strategies (e.g., distillation plus pruning or progressive replacement).

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox of methods for producing compact, deployable models. Contemporary KD techniques include matching logits, aligning internal representations or attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student capacity gaps, task complexity, and data availability. Practical compression typically requires selecting or adapting distilled signals to student capacity and combining complementary methods to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: The Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD can transfer output behavior, intermediate representations, and structural properties from teachers to students. A rich family of methods—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, multi-teacher strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—demonstrate that KD is not a single technique but a design space. The effectiveness of KD depends on factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the nature and complexity of data, task specificity, and availability of unlabeled data; these trade-offs motivate hybrid strategies that combine representation-focused distillation, curriculum-like teacher schedules, and structured pruning to maximize both accuracy and inference efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce compact models that retain much of the performance of large networks by transferring knowledge from one or more teacher models to a student. Research over the last decade has diversified the KD toolkit beyond soft-label supervision to include internal representation matching, adversarial objectives, contrastive and Wasserstein distances, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schemes, teacher-training strategies, and task-aware filter selection. These approaches have been applied across computer vision, NLP (including pretrained Transformers and summarization), retrieval, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Practical trade-offs arise from teacher-student capacity gaps, data requirements, optimization difficulties, and robustness concerns; contemporary work addresses these by narrowing capability gaps (e.g., evolving or student-friendly teachers), selecting or weighting teacher signals, and distilling only task-relevant intermediate features. Empirical studies show that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: the best choice depends on model architectures, target tasks, and constraints on data, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) condenses information from larger, higher-capacity models into smaller, more efficient models to enable deployment under resource constraints. Over the past decade this basic teacher–student framework has diversified: methods transfer logits, hidden/internal representations, attention maps, feature distributions, or policy behavior; teachers may be fixed, jointly trained, or evolved; distillation objectives may use soft-label matching, contrastive or distributional distances, adversarial losses, or curriculum-based schedules. Empirical work demonstrates KD improves compact model performance across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and reinforcement learning, and recent advances target robustness, task-aware filtering, multi-teacher selection, and compression without large unlabeled data. Despite practical successes, open issues remain in choosing what to transfer, matching capacity to distilled data complexity, and reliably transferring robustness and decision-boundary information.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used family of techniques that compress large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. KD has evolved from soft-label matching into many variants—intermediate-representation alignment, contrastive and adversarial objectives, curriculum and route-based supervision, online/multi-teacher strategies, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the type of transferred signal to student capacity and task demands, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques to meet latency, memory, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Remains Central for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Principles, Variants, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a simple teacher-to-student soft-label transfer into a rich family of methods that target robustness, internal representation alignment, task-specific selection of signals, and efficient compression pipelines. Across vision, language, and sequence generation tasks, distillation enables compact models to retain or approach the performance of large models while enabling practical latency and memory benefits. Effective distillation designs combine multiple signals (logits, hidden states, feature correlations), adapt the teacher-student relationship during training, and can be integrated with pruning or module-replacement strategies to achieve strong trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller models to improve compact model quality and efficiency. Across vision, language, retrieval, and sequential decision-making, KD variants include soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and module-replacement strategies, adversarial and contrastive formulations, multi-teacher and teacher-selection methods, online/evolutionary teacher schedules, and task-aware distillation that selects which teacher knowledge to transfer. KD has been combined with structured pruning and other compression approaches to achieve substantial speedups while preserving accuracy. Practical challenges include the teacher–student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, the need for unlabeled data in some pipelines, and retaining robustness or previously learned knowledge in incremental settings. A range of remedies have been proposed: learning student-friendly or adaptive teachers, matching internal feature statistics, confidence-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware layer filters. In practice, distillation has enabled state-of-the-art trade-offs in NLP tasks (classification, summarization, retrieval, machine translation, and non-autoregressive generation), vision tasks, and reinforcement learning, while also being adapted for adversarial robustness and continual learning.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students. Research over the past decade has expanded KD from simple soft-target matching into a wide set of techniques that transfer final outputs, intermediate representations, attention and feature correlations, and decision-boundary information. Practical success depends on choosing which signals to transfer, adapting teacher behavior to student capacity and task constraints, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (e.g., pruning or progressive module replacement) when latency, memory, or robustness demands require hybrid solutions. Despite strong empirical gains across vision and NLP, open challenges remain in reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student capacity gaps and data requirements.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central, versatile technique for producing compact, high-performing models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD succeeds by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and structured behaviors from teachers to students, but no single KD recipe dominates all settings. The most reliable practical approach is hybrid and task-aware: expose informative internal representations, adapt teacher signals to student capacity and the target task, and combine distillation with complementary compression methods such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or targeted robustness procedures to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. The literature shows many complementary algorithmic families — soft-target (logit) transfer, internal-representation and attention/feature matching, contrastive and adversarial objectives, progressive module replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical work across vision, NLP, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning indicates that no single recipe dominates: careful matching of what is distilled to student capacity and task needs, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods tend to give the best accuracy–latency–size trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The field offers a broad, configurable toolkit—ranging from soft-target matching to layer-wise representation alignment, progressive module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning—to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints across vision and NLP applications. Practical success depends on matching the distilled signals to student capacity, task characteristics, and available data.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the last decade the field has evolved from simple soft-target matching to a rich design space that includes logits and intermediate-representation transfer, contrastive and adversarial objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical application is task- and capacity-aware: success depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and data availability, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools where appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, hidden states, feature correlations, decision-boundary information), how teachers are chosen or adapted, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression methods, distillation routinely yields compact models that preserve much of the accuracy of larger models while meeting latency and memory constraints. However, KD is not a single recipe: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity gaps, task characteristics, data availability, and robustness requirements, which motivate task-aware, teacher-aware, and hybrid distillation practices.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and its Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning based models are relatively large, and it is hard to deploy such models on resource-limited devices such as mobile phones and embedded devices. One possible solution is knowledge distillation whereby a smaller model (student model) is trained by utilizing the information from a larger model (teacher model). In this paper, we present a survey of knowledge distillation techniques applied to deep learning models. To compare the performances of different techniques, we propose a new metric called distillation metric. Distillation metric compares different knowledge distillation algorithms based on sizes and accuracy scores. Based on the survey, some interesting conclusions are drawn and presented in this paper.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD delivers consistent gains when its objectives and signals (logits, internal representations, attention maps, contrastive or adversarial losses) are matched to student capacity and task constraints and when it is combined with complementary compression strategies such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. However, KD is not universally optimal: careful teacher design, task-aware signal selection, and hybrid pipelines are often required to realize the best latency–accuracy–robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and How to Use It
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and flexible route to producing compact, high-performance models for deep learning and NLP. When matched to task requirements and student capacity and when combined with complementary compression strategies, distillation routinely yields models that approach the accuracy of large teachers while delivering meaningful latency and memory gains. However, distillation is not universally superior: its benefits depend on what form of knowledge is transferred, the availability and complexity of training data, and the desired properties (e.g., robustness, latency). I argue that distillation should be treated as an indispensable component of a compression toolbox — applied with representation-level signals, teacher-aware adaptations, and hybridization with pruning or progressive replacement when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and indispensable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. The most reliable strategy treats distillation not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox: transfer informative internal representations in addition to soft outputs, adapt or select teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum-based schedules) when latency, memory, or robustness constraints demand it. Distillation can preserve much of teacher accuracy while delivering substantial gains in inference efficiency, but its success requires careful matching of what is transferred, how teachers are adapted, and how complementary methods are integrated.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical design space for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Methods range from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, and feature correlations, and extend to adversarial, contrastive, curriculum, multi-teacher, and meta-learned strategies. Best practices emphasize selecting which teacher signals to transfer, matching distilled information to student capacity and task needs, and combining distillation with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Empirical work across vision, language, ranking, and reinforcement learning shows that task-aware, hybrid distillation pipelines typically deliver the most reliable trade-offs between size, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision and NLP, KD variants transfer information ranging from final soft-labels to intermediate representations, attention maps, and structured feature correlations; practitioners routinely combine distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) and adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task demands. Empirical and theoretical work identifies multiple mechanisms for KD’s effectiveness — better optimization trajectories, regularization-like effects, richer concept learning, and per-instance gradient shaping — while also highlighting important practical factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the availability of unlabeled data, and robustness transfer. Open problems include reliably selecting task-relevant signals to transfer, minimizing unnecessary constraints from mismatched teachers, and integrating distillation with pruning or architectural changes to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, effective distillation is a design space of complementary techniques — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi- or evolving-teacher schedules, student-friendly teacher design, and hybrid pipelines that combine pruning or progressive module replacement. When chosen and combined with attention to teacher–student capacity, task characteristics, and data availability, distillation reliably yields compact models that preserve accuracy and can transfer robustness; when misapplied it can be outperformed by simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or structured pruning strategies. I argue that the best practical posture is to treat distillation as a task-aware hybrid toolbox: prioritize representation-level transfer and teacher engineering, use confidence- or task-aware weighting for multiple signals, integrate robustness-aware objectives when needed, and combine distillation with pruning or module replacement when latency/memory constraints dominate.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Flexible Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a core technique for compressing large models into efficient students for both vision and language tasks. A wide variety of KD formulations — from soft-label transfer and layer-wise matching to adversarial, online, and self-distillation — have demonstrated consistent gains in accuracy, inference speed, and memory footprint. However, distillation is not a single recipe: its effectiveness depends on teacher-student capacity gaps, the form of transferred information (logits, internal representations, attention maps), task characteristics, and data availability. Recent work shows that combining distillation with task-aware filtering, structured pruning, or teacher adaptation yields the best practical tradeoffs. Going forward, hybrid and task-aware distillation strategies that explicitly align representation, decision-boundary, and robustness objectives promise the most reliable compression outcomes.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Indispensable Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware design space rather than a single algorithm. By transferring behavioral and representational signals from larger teachers to smaller students, KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost. When carefully matched to student capacity and task constraints — and when combined with complementary techniques such as pruning, confidence weighting, and targeted representation transfer — KD yields practical, deployable models with strong accuracy–latency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains the most flexible and broadly applicable approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD is best treated as a toolbox: different distillation signals (logits, hidden states, attention/feature correlations), teacher schedules (offline, online/evolutionary, multi-teacher selection), and complementary techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, robustness objectives) should be chosen and combined according to task requirements, student capacity, data availability, and latency or robustness constraints. When KD is designed to align transferred information with student capacity and task needs it yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, NLP, generation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and representational structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. KD has evolved from simple soft-label matching into a configurable toolbox that includes logits matching, intermediate-representation alignment, attention and feature-correlation transfer, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and multi- or online-teacher schedules. When matched to student capacity, task demands, and data availability—and when combined thoughtfully with complementary compression techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement—KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency and resource constraints. However, its effectiveness depends on the form of transferred signals, teacher–student gaps, and robustness or data limitations, motivating hybrid, task-aware designs and continued research into teacher adaptation and training schedules.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most usefully viewed not as a single algorithm but as a configurable, task-aware toolbox. When practitioners select what to transfer (logits, hidden states, attention maps, or structured behaviors), adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or teacher adaptation), KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. However, KD has limits — it depends on data complexity, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the choice of transferred signals — and in some regimes alternative compression strategies can match or exceed distillation unless hybridized thoughtfully.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. The field has evolved from simple soft-label matching to a broad design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on selecting appropriate transfer signals for the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression tools to satisfy constraints on latency, data, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques aim to transfer useful predictive behavior and internal structure from larger, expensive models to smaller, faster models. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, feature distributions, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are coupled (offline, online, multi-teacher, evolutionary, or self-distillation), and what additional objectives or defenses are used (adversarial training, contrastive losses, curriculum-based routing, or geodesic alignment). Distillation has been applied broadly across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding, and interacts with pruning and other compression strategies. Practical trade-offs include the teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness, and the form of supervision needed for good transfer.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods form a broad, task-aware toolbox for turning large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students. The literature spans soft-target (logit) matching, alignment of internal representations and attention, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically requires adapting teacher signals to student capacity, selecting which signals to transfer given task constraints, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox: Essential, Effective, and Bounded
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single soft-label trick into a broad, task-aware toolbox for compressing large deep and NLP models into compact, deployable students. When matched to student capacity, adapted to task constraints, and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning or progressive module replacement), KD routinely produces models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness needs. At the same time, KD has limits tied to data requirements, teacher–student capacity gaps, and robustness transfer; practical deployment benefits from hybrid, selective, and teacher-aware distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models in deep learning and NLP. Its power arises from multiple distinct mechanisms of transfer (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, and training dynamics) and from the flexibility to combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, adversarial objectives, and curriculum schedules). KD is not a universal panacea: its success depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity, adapting teacher signals over training, and considering data, latency, and robustness constraints. Best practice treats KD as a hybrid, task-aware toolbox whose components are chosen and combined to meet the target application’s constraints and goals.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation Remains Central to Model Compression — Best Practice Is a Hybrid, Task-aware Strategy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) continues to be one of the most effective approaches to produce compact, high-performing models for deep learning and NLP. However, KD is not a single recipe: its strengths (soft-target transfer, ensemble compression, and the ability to reshape student training dynamics) come with practical costs and failure modes. Recent work shows structured pruning and alternative compression strategies can match or exceed KD on latency or data-efficiency in some settings. I argue that the best practical path is hybrid: combine KD with task-aware layer-wise methods, internal-representation matching, and targeted robustness or pruning techniques, and choose specific flavors (e.g., multi-teacher, adversarial, progressive replacement, or shrink-and-fine-tune) according to task constraints and available data. The result is compact models that retain accuracy, generalization, and robustness without unnecessary computation or unlabeled-data requirements.
