papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Complementary Tools and Task-Aware Strategies for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central technique for compressing large neural models into efficient students while preserving performance. A growing literature demonstrates a wide array of KD formulations—response-based, feature-based, layer-wise, adversarial, progressive replacing, and online/evolutionary teacher strategies—each addressing specific limitations such as teacher-student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, adversarial vulnerability, data complexity, and continual learning. Distillation should be treated as a toolbox: methods must be chosen and combined according to task demands (e.g., NLP summarization, ranking, detection, or incremental learning) and practical constraints (data availability, latency, and robustness requirements). When combined with structured pruning or task-aware layer filtering, distillation can achieve large speedups with small accuracy loss; in some settings simple shrink-and-fine-tune can also be competitive. Overall, effective compression requires matching the distillation technique to the target task and model constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible family of techniques for transferring the behavior and internal structure of large models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from soft-label matching into a broad design space that includes logits transfer, layer- and feature-wise alignment, attention or correlation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and progressive module replacement. Practical success is task- and capacity-aware: practitioners must choose what to transfer, adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and often combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, module replacement, or shrink-and-fine-tune) to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints. While KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance in many vision and NLP tasks, its effectiveness depends on data complexity, teacher–student gaps, and the choice of transferred signals, and alternative or hybrid pipelines can be preferable in some regimes.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. A broad range of KD techniques—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filters, multi-teacher strategies, teacher-side learning, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—has proven effective across vision, retrieval, generation and NLP tasks. However, distillation has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, dataset complexity, and robustness; these limits can be mitigated by adapting the distillation signal (e.g., via routing, confidence weighting, evolution or self-distillation), aligning internal representations selectively for the target task, or combining distillation with structured pruning. Taken together, the literature shows that KD is not a single recipe but a design space; careful matching of distillation strategy to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints yields the best compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. The literature shows KD is not a single recipe but a design space of techniques (logits, internal representations, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules) that, when matched to student capacity and task demands and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), yield strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective practice requires selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to the student, and hybridizing distillation with pruning or architecture-aware replacement where appropriate; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. The literature shows many complementary algorithmic families — soft-target (logit) transfer, internal-representation and attention/feature matching, contrastive and adversarial objectives, progressive module replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical work across vision, NLP, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning indicates that no single recipe dominates: careful matching of what is distilled to student capacity and task needs, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods tend to give the best accuracy–latency–size trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the last decade KD has expanded from soft-target matching into a rich toolkit that includes internal-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred information to student capacity and task constraints, and on making teacher signals student-friendly. KD is therefore best used as a task-aware toolbox rather than a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. When designed to match what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations), how teachers and students are coupled (teacher engineering, online or multi-teacher schemes, curriculum or route-based schedules), and when combined with complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement), KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and robustness requirements. However, the practical success of KD depends on matching transfer signals to student capacity and task demands, managing teacher–student capacity gaps, and addressing data and robustness constraints; in some settings, alternative or hybrid compression strategies may be preferable.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical design space for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students so that compact models approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. The literature documents many distinct signals (soft outputs, hidden states, attention and feature correlations), coupling strategies (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, curriculum schedules), and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Success depends on choosing what to transfer to match student capacity and task needs, managing teacher–student gaps and data availability, and integrating robustness and latency considerations. Empirical work across classification, generation, retrieval, continual learning, and reinforcement learning shows KD is indispensable for many compression problems but must be applied task-awarely and often in combination with complementary compression methods.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and indispensable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. The most reliable strategy treats distillation not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox: transfer informative internal representations in addition to soft outputs, adapt or select teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum-based schedules) when latency, memory, or robustness constraints demand it. Distillation can preserve much of teacher accuracy while delivering substantial gains in inference efficiency, but its success requires careful matching of what is transferred, how teachers are adapted, and how complementary methods are integrated.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: The Role of Knowledge Distillation in Compressing Deep and NLP Models: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable models. It works through multiple mechanisms — soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, and structured guidance — and can be adapted via curriculum strategies, multi-teacher weighting, adversarial or decision-boundary-aware examples, and progressive module replacement. Distillation often yields models that approach teacher accuracy while improving latency and memory, but its success depends on matching distillation methods to task properties and model capacity; in some settings structured pruning or hybrid approaches can match or exceed distillation without the need for large unlabeled corpora. I argue that distillation is indispensable for practical NLP and deep learning deployments when used with task-aware, representation-level, and teacher-aware strategies, and that combining distillation with complementary compression methods yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its strength lies in a broad design space — from soft-target matching to representation-level alignment, multi-teacher and student-friendly teacher strategies, and adversarial or robustness-aware objectives — which, when combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacement), yields the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective deployment requires selecting what to transfer and how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints rather than applying a single off-the-shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. The field has evolved from simple soft-label matching to a broad design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on selecting appropriate transfer signals for the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression tools to satisfy constraints on latency, data, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and flexible family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. The literature treats KD as a design space rather than a single recipe: practitioners transfer soft logits, internal representations, attention/feature statistics, or training dynamics; they use offline, online/evolving, multi-teacher, or self-distillation schedules; and they often combine KD with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective distillation aligns the form and amount of transferred information with student capacity and task needs, and best practice is task-aware, hybrid, and selective about what to copy from the teacher.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: A Distillation-First Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single recipe. Best results arise from (1) transferring internal, structured representations in addition to logits, (2) adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and (3) combining distillation with complementary compression strategies such as progressive module replacement or structured pruning. This position synthesizes empirical and algorithmic advances to recommend practical design patterns for building compact, robust models for deployment in vision, language, and reinforcement-learning settings.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. KD succeeds not because it is a single fixed recipe but because it is a design space: practitioners can choose what signals to transfer (logits, intermediate features, feature correlations, or decision-boundary information), how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and whether to combine distillation with complementary techniques such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. KD yields consistent gains when matched to task constraints and student capacity, but it has limits — notably sensitivity to teacher–student gaps, data complexity, and some robustness-transfer failures — that motivate hybrid, task-aware strategies and careful teacher engineering.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Methods span soft-label (logit) matching, alignment of intermediate representations and attention maps, teacher design strategies (offline, online, multi- or evolving teachers), adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum or confidence-weighted schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective application requires matching what is distilled to the student’s capacity, adapting teacher signals to task constraints and data availability, and often combining distillation with complementary compression methods to meet latency, robustness, and data-budget goals.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most usefully viewed not as a single algorithm but as a configurable, task-aware toolbox. When practitioners select what to transfer (logits, hidden states, attention maps, or structured behaviors), adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or teacher adaptation), KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. However, KD has limits — it depends on data complexity, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the choice of transferred signals — and in some regimes alternative compression strategies can match or exceed distillation unless hybridized thoughtfully.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practically indispensable approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox and combined with complementary techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, confidence weighting, and teacher adaptation), distillation routinely delivers favorable accuracy–latency trade-offs. However, its effectiveness depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, addressing teacher–student gaps, considering data and compute constraints, and explicitly accounting for robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: On Learning the Geodesic Path for Incremental Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Neural networks notoriously suffer from the problem of catastrophic forgetting, the phenomenon of forgetting the past knowledge when acquiring new knowledge. Overcoming catastrophic forgetting is of significant importance to emulate the process of "incremental learning", where the model is capable of learning from sequential experience in an efficient and robust way. State-of-the-art techniques for incremental learning make use of knowledge distillation towards preventing catastrophic forgetting. Therein, one updates the network while ensuring that the network's responses to previously seen concepts remain stable throughout updates. This in practice is done by minimizing the dissimilarity between current and previous responses of the network one way or another. Our work contributes a novel method to the arsenal of distillation techniques. In contrast to the previous state of the art, we propose to firstly construct low-dimensional manifolds for previous and current responses and minimize the dissimilarity between the responses along the geodesic connecting the manifolds. This induces a more formidable knowledge distillation with smooth properties which preserves the past knowledge more efficiently as observed by our comprehensive empirical study.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision and NLP, KD variants transfer information ranging from final soft-labels to intermediate representations, attention maps, and structured feature correlations; practitioners routinely combine distillation with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) and adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task demands. Empirical and theoretical work identifies multiple mechanisms for KD’s effectiveness — better optimization trajectories, regularization-like effects, richer concept learning, and per-instance gradient shaping — while also highlighting important practical factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the availability of unlabeled data, and robustness transfer. Open problems include reliably selecting task-relevant signals to transfer, minimizing unnecessary constraints from mismatched teachers, and integrating distillation with pruning or architectural changes to maximize latency and accuracy tradeoffs.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller models to improve compact model quality and efficiency. Across vision, language, retrieval, and sequential decision-making, KD variants include soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and module-replacement strategies, adversarial and contrastive formulations, multi-teacher and teacher-selection methods, online/evolutionary teacher schedules, and task-aware distillation that selects which teacher knowledge to transfer. KD has been combined with structured pruning and other compression approaches to achieve substantial speedups while preserving accuracy. Practical challenges include the teacher–student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, the need for unlabeled data in some pipelines, and retaining robustness or previously learned knowledge in incremental settings. A range of remedies have been proposed: learning student-friendly or adaptive teachers, matching internal feature statistics, confidence-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware layer filters. In practice, distillation has enabled state-of-the-art trade-offs in NLP tasks (classification, summarization, retrieval, machine translation, and non-autoregressive generation), vision tasks, and reinforcement learning, while also being adapted for adversarial robustness and continual learning.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring functional behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from soft-target supervision into a rich toolbox that includes internal-representation alignment, attention/feature matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective compression is task- and constraint-aware: the best choices depend on what signals are transferred, how teachers are constructed or adapted, student capacity, available data, and deployment constraints (latency, memory, and robustness). While KD often yields strong accuracy–latency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks, remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, reducing heavy distillation data or compute needs, and selecting task-relevant intermediate signals.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: The Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD can transfer output behavior, intermediate representations, and structural properties from teachers to students. A rich family of methods—soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, multi-teacher strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines—demonstrate that KD is not a single technique but a design space. The effectiveness of KD depends on factors such as teacher–student capacity gap, the nature and complexity of data, task specificity, and availability of unlabeled data; these trade-offs motivate hybrid strategies that combine representation-focused distillation, curriculum-like teacher schedules, and structured pruning to maximize both accuracy and inference efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The primary goal of knowledge distillation (KD) is to encapsulate the information of a model learned from a teacher network into a student network, with the latter being more compact than the former. Existing work, e.g., using Kullback-Leibler divergence for distillation, may fail to capture important structural knowledge in the teacher network and often lacks the ability for feature generalization, particularly in situations when teacher and student are built to address different classification tasks. We propose Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation (WCoRD), which leverages both primal and dual forms of Wasserstein distance for KD. The dual form is used for global knowledge transfer, yielding a contrastive learning objective that maximizes the lower bound of mutual information between the teacher and the student networks. The primal form is used for local contrastive knowledge transfer within a mini-batch, effectively matching the distributions of features between the teacher and the student networks. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed WCoRD method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on privileged information distillation, model compression and cross-modal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates information from large, high-capacity models into smaller, more efficient student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, and memory constraints. Over the past decade KD evolved from simple soft-target matching to a broad design space that includes internal-representation alignment, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results across vision and NLP tasks (classification, retrieval, summarization, translation, and non-autoregressive generation) show that carefully selected or combined distillation strategies can substantially close the performance gap to teachers while delivering large reductions in size or latency. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how teachers and students are coupled to student capacity, task complexity, and data availability; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing which intermediate signals are task-relevant, and avoiding unnecessary constraints from overconfident or mismatched teachers.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible family of techniques for transferring the behavior and internal structure of large models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from soft-label matching into a broad design space that includes logits transfer, layer- and feature-wise alignment, attention or correlation matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and progressive module replacement. Practical success is task- and capacity-aware: practitioners must choose what to transfer, adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and often combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, module replacement, or shrink-and-fine-tune) to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints. While KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance in many vision and NLP tasks, its effectiveness depends on data complexity, teacher–student gaps, and the choice of transferred signals, and alternative or hybrid pipelines can be preferable in some regimes.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Principles, Variants, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied approach for compressing large neural networks into smaller, deployable models by transferring functional behavior and internal structure from teacher models to students. Over the past decade KD has diversified beyond soft-label supervision into a design space that includes intermediate-representation matching, multi- and online-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, evolutionary teachers, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD improves compact model performance across vision and NLP tasks (including pretrained transformer compression, machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, and continual learning), but its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity gap, availability of data, and task-specific constraints. Best practice is task-aware: select appropriate target signals (logits, hidden states, attention or features), manage capacity gaps via teacher adaptation or evolving teachers, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques when latency or data limits dominate.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. The literature shows many complementary algorithmic families — soft-target (logit) transfer, internal-representation and attention/feature matching, contrastive and adversarial objectives, progressive module replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical work across vision, NLP, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning indicates that no single recipe dominates: careful matching of what is distilled to student capacity and task needs, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods tend to give the best accuracy–latency–size trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical design space for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students so that compact models approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. The literature documents many distinct signals (soft outputs, hidden states, attention and feature correlations), coupling strategies (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, curriculum schedules), and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Success depends on choosing what to transfer to match student capacity and task needs, managing teacher–student gaps and data availability, and integrating robustness and latency considerations. Empirical work across classification, generation, retrieval, continual learning, and reinforcement learning shows KD is indispensable for many compression problems but must be applied task-awarely and often in combination with complementary compression methods.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods form a large, well-developed design space for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, faster students or compact subnetworks. The literature documents many complementary approaches — soft-target matching, intermediate representation alignment, layer- and task-aware filters, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schedules, and hybrid pruning–distillation pipelines — and evaluates them across NLP, machine translation, summarization, retrieval, vision, and sequential decision tasks. Practical success depends on choosing what to transfer, how to adapt teacher signals to student capacity and task needs, and how to combine distillation with pruning or module replacement to meet latency and robustness constraints. Ongoing challenges highlight the need for task-aware representational targets, student-friendly teacher design, and methods that avoid heavy reliance on large unlabeled corpora while preserving robustness and efficient inference.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD delivers consistent gains when its objectives and signals (logits, internal representations, attention maps, contrastive or adversarial losses) are matched to student capacity and task constraints and when it is combined with complementary compression strategies such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. However, KD is not universally optimal: careful teacher design, task-aware signal selection, and hybrid pipelines are often required to realize the best latency–accuracy–robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes the state of knowledge distillation (KD) and its role in model compression for deep learning and NLP. It surveys what is transferred from teachers to students (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, and training dynamics), how teachers and students are coupled (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive/evolving schemes), the principal mechanisms by which distillation benefits students (label smoothing, reduced data complexity, representation shaping, and gradient/decision-boundary effects), common applications across NLP tasks, empirical practicalities and trade-offs (teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness transfer, and compute/latency constraints), and recommended task-aware, hybrid practices that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. The synthesis also highlights recurring open challenges such as reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant teacher signals for a given student capacity, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, effective distillation is a design space of complementary techniques — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi- or evolving-teacher schedules, student-friendly teacher design, and hybrid pipelines that combine pruning or progressive module replacement. When chosen and combined with attention to teacher–student capacity, task characteristics, and data availability, distillation reliably yields compact models that preserve accuracy and can transfer robustness; when misapplied it can be outperformed by simpler shrink-and-fine-tune or structured pruning strategies. I argue that the best practical posture is to treat distillation as a task-aware hybrid toolbox: prioritize representation-level transfer and teacher engineering, use confidence- or task-aware weighting for multiple signals, integrate robustness-aware objectives when needed, and combine distillation with pruning or module replacement when latency/memory constraints dominate.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Toolbox: Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategies for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students, but its success hinges on matching the distillation strategy to task demands, student capacity, and data constraints. Rather than a single recipe, KD should be treated as a flexible toolbox combining soft-labels, internal-representation alignment, teacher adaptation, layer-wise filtering, adversarial objectives, and pruning or module-replacement where appropriate. When chosen and combined thoughtfully—exposing informative internal signals, adapting teacher supervision to student capacity, and using task-aware selection—KD yields compact models that retain high performance, robustness, and practical latency gains.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Baker

Methods range from soft-target matching to internal-representation alignment, progressive module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or task-aware filtering. Empirical evidence across natural language tasks (classification, summarization, translation, retrieval) and other domains shows that KD can preserve or approach teacher performance while improving latency and memory, but its success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, data complexity, and task constraints.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller models to improve compact model quality and efficiency. Across vision, language, retrieval, and sequential decision-making, KD variants include soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and module-replacement strategies, adversarial and contrastive formulations, multi-teacher and teacher-selection methods, online/evolutionary teacher schedules, and task-aware distillation that selects which teacher knowledge to transfer. KD has been combined with structured pruning and other compression approaches to achieve substantial speedups while preserving accuracy. Practical challenges include the teacher–student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, the need for unlabeled data in some pipelines, and retaining robustness or previously learned knowledge in incremental settings. A range of remedies have been proposed: learning student-friendly or adaptive teachers, matching internal feature statistics, confidence-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware layer filters. In practice, distillation has enabled state-of-the-art trade-offs in NLP tasks (classification, summarization, retrieval, machine translation, and non-autoregressive generation), vision tasks, and reinforcement learning, while also being adapted for adversarial robustness and continual learning.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has broadened from soft-label matching to include representation-level transfer, multi- and evolving-teacher schedules, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Its effectiveness depends on choosing what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and combining complementary compression techniques when data, latency, or robustness demands require it. Best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox rather than a single recipe.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models by transferring useful predictive behavior and internal structure from teacher models to smaller students. The field encompasses a wide spectrum of techniques — matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, layer-wise or module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher strategies, and combinations with structured pruning — each suited to different capacity gaps, data regimes, latency constraints, and robustness needs. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation helps by smoothing supervision, reducing data complexity, shaping per-instance gradients and decision boundaries, and providing representational priors that smaller models can exploit. Effective compression typically requires choosing or adapting what is transferred to the student's capacity and the target task, and often benefits from hybrid strategies (e.g., distillation plus pruning or progressive replacement).

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used family of techniques that compress large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. KD has evolved from soft-label matching into many variants—intermediate-representation alignment, contrastive and adversarial objectives, curriculum and route-based supervision, online/multi-teacher strategies, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Practical success depends on matching the type of transferred signal to student capacity and task demands, adapting teacher signals during training, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques to meet latency, memory, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger models to smaller ones to improve efficiency while preserving or enhancing performance. Research has explored why distillation works, how to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information), and how to adapt distillation to settings such as multi-teacher ensembles, continual/incremental learning, task-specific compression, and robustness. A rich set of algorithmic families has emerged — including layer-wise and module-replacement schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, teacher-student co-training and evolution, pruning combined with distillation, and task-aware filtering — each addressing capacity gaps, representation mismatch, or computational constraints in different ways. Empirical studies across vision, NLP (including machine translation, summarization, and dense retrieval), reinforcement learning, and 3D detection demonstrate both substantial gains and important failure modes, motivating continued work on matching distilled information to student capacity and task requirements.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings by transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller ones, or by producing compact subnetworks via pruning. Across vision, language, ranking, and sequential learning tasks the literature has diversified into methods that match outputs, internal representations, or training dynamics; that use single, multiple, evolving, or self-supervising teachers; and that integrate adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-like strategies. Empirical results show that careful design of the teacher-student interaction, attention to the capacity gap, and task-aware selection of distilled knowledge often determine success. Hybrid approaches that combine distillation with pruning, module replacement, or robustness-aware objectives can yield compact models that preserve accuracy and, in some cases, adversarial robustness or continual-learning stability.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolkit for producing compact models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD improves student performance by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and training dynamics, but its success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, task demands, and deployment constraints. Best practice treats KD as part of a hybrid compression pipeline—selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement when needed.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Toolbox: Practical Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When applied as a toolbox — combining soft-target supervision, intermediate-representation alignment, teacher engineering, adversarial or robustness-aware objectives, and, when appropriate, structured pruning or progressive module replacement — distillation routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while improving latency and memory. Its success depends on matching methods to the teacher–student capacity gap, task demands, and data availability; in some deployment regimes simpler compress-and-fine-tune or pruning-first strategies can be competitive. I argue that practitioners should treat distillation as a configurable set of techniques chosen to fit task constraints rather than a single off‑the‑shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible, task-aware approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. The field treats distillation as a toolbox of methods—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, using contrastive/adversarial objectives, and employing multi- or online-teacher schedules—often in hybrid pipelines together with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, choosing suitable teacher schedules, and integrating complementary compression techniques when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce compact models that retain much of the performance of large networks by transferring knowledge from one or more teacher models to a student. Research over the last decade has diversified the KD toolkit beyond soft-label supervision to include internal representation matching, adversarial objectives, contrastive and Wasserstein distances, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schemes, teacher-training strategies, and task-aware filter selection. These approaches have been applied across computer vision, NLP (including pretrained Transformers and summarization), retrieval, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Practical trade-offs arise from teacher-student capacity gaps, data requirements, optimization difficulties, and robustness concerns; contemporary work addresses these by narrowing capability gaps (e.g., evolving or student-friendly teachers), selecting or weighting teacher signals, and distilling only task-relevant intermediate features. Empirical studies show that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: the best choice depends on model architectures, target tasks, and constraints on data, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible set of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to achieve deployable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Rather than a single recipe, KD comprises response-based, representation-based, adversarial, and meta- or multi-teacher methods that should be chosen and combined according to student capacity, task demands, and available data. When designed with task-aware choices of transferred signals and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance; however, success requires careful management of teacher–student mismatch, data requirements, and robustness transfer.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. By selecting what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or structured behaviors), adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or teacher adaptation), practitioners can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Effective compression requires matching distillation strategies to task demands, data availability, and deployment constraints; blindly applying a single distillation recipe risks wasted effort or suboptimal trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a task-aware, hybrid toolbox: designers should select which teacher signals to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, or training dynamics), adapt teacher supervision to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or module-substitution schedules). When these design choices are matched to task constraints and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness requirements. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant internal signals, and closing large teacher–student capacity gaps without overconstraining the student.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that success depends less on a single canonical loss and more on how teacher knowledge is selected, represented, and adapted to the student and the target task. Best results arise when distillation methods (1) expose informative internal representations rather than only final logits, (2) adapt or curate teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and (3) combine distillation with complementary compression strategies (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement). When applied with attention to these aspects, distillation yields compact models that maintain high accuracy, can inherit robustness, and scale to practical inference budgets.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques provide a flexible design space for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students. Methods include soft-target (logit) matching, internal-representation alignment, layer- or module-wise replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, confidence- or curriculum-weighted supervision, and adversarial or contrastive objectives. Empirical results across vision and NLP show that combining representation-level transfer with teacher engineering and complementary compression (pruning or progressive replacement) typically yields the best trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and model size. Success depends on matching what is distilled to student capacity, adapting teacher signals to task constraints, and accounting for data complexity and robustness needs.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Remains Central for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Principles, Variants, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a simple teacher-to-student soft-label transfer into a rich family of methods that target robustness, internal representation alignment, task-specific selection of signals, and efficient compression pipelines. Across vision, language, and sequence generation tasks, distillation enables compact models to retain or approach the performance of large models while enabling practical latency and memory benefits. Effective distillation designs combine multiple signals (logits, hidden states, feature correlations), adapt the teacher-student relationship during training, and can be integrated with pruning or module-replacement strategies to achieve strong trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains the most flexible and broadly applicable approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD is best treated as a toolbox: different distillation signals (logits, hidden states, attention/feature correlations), teacher schedules (offline, online/evolutionary, multi-teacher selection), and complementary techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, robustness objectives) should be chosen and combined according to task requirements, student capacity, data availability, and latency or robustness constraints. When KD is designed to align transferred information with student capacity and task needs it yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, NLP, generation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and indispensable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. The most reliable strategy treats distillation not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox: transfer informative internal representations in addition to soft outputs, adapt or select teacher signals to match student capacity and task needs, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, or curriculum-based schedules) when latency, memory, or robustness constraints demand it. Distillation can preserve much of teacher accuracy while delivering substantial gains in inference efficiency, but its success requires careful matching of what is transferred, how teachers are adapted, and how complementary methods are integrated.
