papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation via Route Constrained Optimization
papers_seen.abstract: Distillation-based learning boosts the performance of the miniaturized neural network based on the hypothesis that the representation of a teacher model can be used as structured and relatively weak supervision, and thus would be easily learned by a miniaturized model. However, we find that the representation of a converged heavy model is still a strong constraint for training a small student model, which leads to a high lower bound of congruence loss. In this work, inspired by curriculum learning we consider the knowledge distillation from the perspective of curriculum learning by routing. Instead of supervising the student model with a converged teacher model, we supervised it with some anchor points selected from the route in parameter space that the teacher model passed by, as we called route constrained optimization (RCO). We experimentally demonstrate this simple operation greatly reduces the lower bound of congruence loss for knowledge distillation, hint and mimicking learning. On close-set classification tasks like CIFAR100 and ImageNet, RCO improves knowledge distillation by 2.14% and 1.5% respectively. For the sake of evaluating the generalization, we also test RCO on the open-set face recognition task MegaFace.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer useful predictive behavior from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students) while preserving accuracy and often adding desirable properties such as robustness or task-specific efficiency. A wide range of methods has been developed: soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer- or module-wise compression, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, and hybrid approaches that combine pruning with distillation. Empirical results across vision, language, ranking, summarization, and reinforcement learning show that carefully chosen distillation strategies can reclaim much of a teacher's performance in a compact student, but outcomes depend strongly on the choice of distilled signals, the alignment of capacities, teacher selection or adaptation, and task-specific constraints. Recent work also emphasizes robustness transfer, task-aware filtering of teacher signals, and alternatives to distillation such as structured pruning that can match distillation in latency without extra unlabeled data. Remaining challenges include principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer, scaling to diverse prediction tasks, and combining distillation with compression and robustness objectives in a computationally efficient way.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Task-Aware Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger models (teachers) into smaller models (students) to achieve deployable efficiency. The literature has expanded from simple soft-label matching to a broad toolbox that includes logits and intermediate-representation transfer, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, progressive module replacement, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning or module replacement. Empirical and analytic work shows that effectiveness depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity, the target task, and available data; combining complementary compression tools often yields the best practical trade-offs. Open challenges include the teacher–student capacity gap, reliable transfer of robustness, and minimizing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible set of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to achieve deployable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Rather than a single recipe, KD comprises response-based, representation-based, adversarial, and meta- or multi-teacher methods that should be chosen and combined according to student capacity, task demands, and available data. When designed with task-aware choices of transferred signals and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), distillation routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance; however, success requires careful management of teacher–student mismatch, data requirements, and robustness transfer.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Its strengths arise from multiple complementary mechanisms (soft targets, internal representation transfer, teacher engineering, and supervised schedules), and the most reliable practical strategies treat KD as a configurable toolbox that is combined with pruning or module replacement when deployment constraints demand it. Practitioners obtain the best trade-offs by matching distilled signals to student capacity, adapting teacher dynamics to the task, and using hybrid pipelines tailored to data, latency, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Work across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding shows KD variants — from soft-label matching to internal-representation alignment, teacher adaptation, adversarial and curriculum-based schedules, and hybrid pipelines combining pruning or module replacement — routinely recover much of teacher performance when the distillation strategy is matched to task demands and student capacity. Important limitations remain: sensitivity to teacher–student capacity gaps, reliance on unlabeled data and heavy distillation compute in some pipelines, and uneven transfer of robustness, motivating continued research into targeted transfer signals and efficient, student-aware distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical design space for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students so that compact models approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. The literature documents many distinct signals (soft outputs, hidden states, attention and feature correlations), coupling strategies (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, curriculum schedules), and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. Success depends on choosing what to transfer to match student capacity and task needs, managing teacher–student gaps and data availability, and integrating robustness and latency considerations. Empirical work across classification, generation, retrieval, continual learning, and reinforcement learning shows KD is indispensable for many compression problems but must be applied task-awarely and often in combination with complementary compression methods.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible design space that, when used with task-aware choices and complementary compression techniques, enables practical model compression for deep learning and NLP. Distillation can preserve much of a teacher's accuracy while cutting inference cost, but its success depends on selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task needs, and combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement when latency and memory are critical.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox of methods for producing compact, deployable models. Contemporary KD techniques include matching logits, aligning internal representations or attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student capacity gaps, task complexity, and data availability. Practical compression typically requires selecting or adapting distilled signals to student capacity and combining complementary methods to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central and Complementary Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a versatile and effective approach for compressing large models into compact, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD’s strengths arise from its ability to transfer soft targets, internal representations, and task-relevant signals to reshape student training dynamics, and it admits many practical variants (multi-teacher, adversarial, curriculum, online/evolutionary, and progressive replacement). At the same time, structured pruning and module-replacement methods can be competitive or complementary when latency, data, or compute constraints dominate. Best practice is a toolbox mentality: choose what to transfer to match student capacity, adapt the teacher–student relationship during training, and combine distillation with pruning or curriculum strategies when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones across vision and NLP. The literature provides many complementary distillation objectives and workflows — soft-label transfer, intermediate-representation matching, adversarial/contrastive losses, online and multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Effectiveness depends strongly on teacher–student capacity gaps, the exact form of transferred information, task characteristics, and data availability; best practice is to select or adapt distillation signals to the student and downstream task and to combine methods where appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: A Distillation-First Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most effective when treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single recipe. Best results arise from (1) transferring internal, structured representations in addition to logits, (2) adapting teacher signals to student capacity and task constraints, and (3) combining distillation with complementary compression strategies such as progressive module replacement or structured pruning. This position synthesizes empirical and algorithmic advances to recommend practical design patterns for building compact, robust models for deployment in vision, language, and reinforcement-learning settings.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and How to Use It
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and flexible route to producing compact, high-performance models for deep learning and NLP. When matched to task requirements and student capacity and when combined with complementary compression strategies, distillation routinely yields models that approach the accuracy of large teachers while delivering meaningful latency and memory gains. However, distillation is not universally superior: its benefits depend on what form of knowledge is transferred, the availability and complexity of training data, and the desired properties (e.g., robustness, latency). I argue that distillation should be treated as an indispensable component of a compression toolbox — applied with representation-level signals, teacher-aware adaptations, and hybridization with pruning or progressive replacement when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Koch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, task-aware design space for transferring behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. The field has expanded from soft-label matching to include intermediate-representation matching, layer-wise/task-aware filtering, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, evolutionary and online teachers, and progressive module replacement. KD is most effective when chosen and combined according to task constraints, student capacity, data availability, and goals (latency, memory, or robustness); complementary techniques such as structured pruning or progressive replacement are often used alongside KD to meet deployment requirements. Empirical work shows that, when applied thoughtfully, KD can produce compact models that recover much of teacher performance while delivering meaningful reductions in parameter count and inference cost, though open challenges remain around teacher–student gaps, robustness transfer, and data-limited regimes.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models in deep learning and NLP. Its power arises from multiple distinct mechanisms of transfer (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/feature maps, and training dynamics) and from the flexibility to combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, adversarial objectives, and curriculum schedules). KD is not a universal panacea: its success depends on matching what is transferred to student capacity, adapting teacher signals over training, and considering data, latency, and robustness constraints. Best practice treats KD as a hybrid, task-aware toolbox whose components are chosen and combined to meet the target application’s constraints and goals.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. The literature shows many complementary algorithmic families — soft-target (logit) transfer, internal-representation and attention/feature matching, contrastive and adversarial objectives, progressive module replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical work across vision, NLP, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning indicates that no single recipe dominates: careful matching of what is distilled to student capacity and task needs, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods tend to give the best accuracy–latency–size trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most usefully viewed not as a single algorithm but as a configurable, task-aware toolbox. When practitioners select what to transfer (logits, hidden states, attention maps, or structured behaviors), adapt teacher signals to student capacity, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or teacher adaptation), KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and robustness constraints. However, KD has limits — it depends on data complexity, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the choice of transferred signals — and in some regimes alternative compression strategies can match or exceed distillation unless hybridized thoughtfully.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring functional behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD evolved from soft-target supervision into a rich toolbox that includes internal-representation alignment, attention/feature matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective compression is task- and constraint-aware: the best choices depend on what signals are transferred, how teachers are constructed or adapted, student capacity, available data, and deployment constraints (latency, memory, and robustness). While KD often yields strong accuracy–latency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks, remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, reducing heavy distillation data or compute needs, and selecting task-relevant intermediate signals.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Distilling Dense Representations for Ranking using Tightly-Coupled Teachers
papers_seen.abstract: We present an approach to ranking with dense representations that applies knowledge distillation to improve the recently proposed late-interaction ColBERT model. Specifically, we distill the knowledge from ColBERT's expressive MaxSim operator for computing relevance scores into a simple dot product, thus enabling single-step ANN search. Our key insight is that during distillation, tight coupling between the teacher model and the student model enables more flexible distillation strategies and yields better learned representations. We empirically show that our approach improves query latency and greatly reduces the onerous storage requirements of ColBERT, while only making modest sacrifices in terms of effectiveness. By combining our dense representations with sparse representations derived from document expansion, we are able to approach the effectiveness of a standard cross-encoder reranker using BERT that is orders of magnitude slower.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. The literature shows KD is not a single recipe but a design space of techniques (logits, internal representations, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules) that, when matched to student capacity and task demands and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), yield strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective practice requires selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to the student, and hybridizing distillation with pruning or architecture-aware replacement where appropriate; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavioral and representational knowledge from teacher models. The field has diversified from simple soft-target matching to a rich design space that includes internal-representation alignment, multi- and evolving-teacher schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, confidence- and task-aware weighting, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, addressing teacher–student gaps, and combining distillation with complementary compression strategies when data or latency constraints demand it.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central and Complementary Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical, versatile, and central approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones across vision and NLP. KD can transfer outputs, internal representations, and structure from teacher to student, and—when combined with task-aware selection, adaptive teacher schedules, or structured pruning—yields strong trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. However, KD has limits tied to teacher–student capacity gaps, data and compute requirements, and potential optimization mismatches; these limits motivate hybrid pipelines and careful design choices that match what is distilled to the student’s capacity and the target application.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring outputs, internal representations, and training dynamics from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, task-aware layer-wise filtering, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and analytical work across vision and NLP shows that distillation, when matched to student capacity and task constraints and often combined with complementary compression methods, reliably improves compact-model performance while exposing remaining challenges in robustness, data requirements, and teacher–student mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Indispensable Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and versatile approach for compressing large models into compact, deployable students in vision and NLP. KD is best treated as a configurable, task-aware toolbox that transfers logits, internal representations, attention or feature structure, and can be combined with teacher engineering, multi-teacher or online schedules, adversarial/contrastive objectives, and complementary compression such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. When matched to student capacity, task demands, and deployment constraints, KD routinely yields strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness; however, limits remain related to teacher–student capacity gaps, data requirements, and reliable robustness transfer. Practical success comes from task-aware selection of signals, adaptive teacher strategies, and hybrid pipelines that incorporate pruning or module replacement when necessary.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a broadly useful and adaptable family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP, KD methods extend beyond soft-target matching to include internal-representation transfer, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how it is transferred to student capacity, task properties, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains the most flexible and broadly applicable approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD is best treated as a toolbox: different distillation signals (logits, hidden states, attention/feature correlations), teacher schedules (offline, online/evolutionary, multi-teacher selection), and complementary techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, robustness objectives) should be chosen and combined according to task requirements, student capacity, data availability, and latency or robustness constraints. When KD is designed to align transferred information with student capacity and task needs it yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, NLP, generation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices (Synthesis)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for producing compact, deployable deep models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students. Over the last decade KD diversified from simple soft-label transfer into many variants that match logits, internal representations, attention/feature maps, or training dynamics, and that interact with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning and progressive module replacement. Practical deployment benefits most from hybrid, task-aware strategies that select what to transfer, adapt the teacher-student relationship, and combine distillation with pruning or architectural replacement to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. When treated as a toolbox—covering soft-label transfer, intermediate-representation matching, multi-teacher schedules, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and integrations with pruning or module replacement—KD reliably reduces model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. Its effectiveness depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, adapting teacher dynamics, and accounting for data and robustness constraints. KD is indispensable for many practical deployments, but practitioners should combine it with complementary compression strategies and task-aware design to navigate limits posed by capacity gaps, data scarcity, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Mechanisms, Variants, Task Considerations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring useful information from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple soft-target matching into a rich set of methods that transfer logits, intermediate representations, feature correlations, and decision-boundary information; use single, multiple, evolving, or learned teachers; and combine with pruning or module replacement. Practical success depends on aligning what is transferred to student capacity and task requirements, and best results typically come from hybrid, task-aware strategies that match distillation signals to model and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD's strength derives from a flexible design space — transferring logits, intermediate representations, attention or feature correlations, and decision-boundary information — and from compatibility with complementary strategies such as structured pruning, progressive module replacement, and teacher adaptation. While KD does not universally dominate every setting, when applied in a task-aware, representation-focused, and teacher-aware way it reliably yields compact models that approach teacher performance while delivering practical latency, memory, and robustness benefits.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes the state of knowledge distillation (KD) and its role in model compression for deep learning and NLP. It surveys what is transferred from teachers to students (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/feature correlations, and training dynamics), how teachers and students are coupled (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and progressive/evolving schemes), the principal mechanisms by which distillation benefits students (label smoothing, reduced data complexity, representation shaping, and gradient/decision-boundary effects), common applications across NLP tasks, empirical practicalities and trade-offs (teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness transfer, and compute/latency constraints), and recommended task-aware, hybrid practices that combine distillation with pruning or module replacement. The synthesis also highlights recurring open challenges such as reliably transferring robustness, selecting task-relevant teacher signals for a given student capacity, and reducing dependence on large unlabeled corpora.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Improving Multi-Task Deep Neural Networks via Knowledge Distillation for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: This paper explores the use of knowledge distillation to improve a Multi-Task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) (Liu et al., 2019) for learning text representations across multiple natural language understanding tasks. Although ensemble learning can improve model performance, serving an ensemble of large DNNs such as MT-DNN can be prohibitively expensive. Here we apply the knowledge distillation method (Hinton et al., 2015) in the multi-task learning setting. For each task, we train an ensemble of different MT-DNNs (teacher) that outperforms any single model, and then train a single MT-DNN (student) via multi-task learning to \emph{distill} knowledge from these ensemble teachers. We show that the distilled MT-DNN significantly outperforms the original MT-DNN on 7 out of 9 GLUE tasks, pushing the GLUE benchmark (single model) to 83.7\% (1.5\% absolute improvement\footnote{ Based on the GLUE leaderboard at https://gluebenchmark.com/leaderboard as of April 1, 2019.}). The code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available at https://github.com/namisan/mt-dnn.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and flexible family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. The literature treats KD as a design space rather than a single recipe: practitioners transfer soft logits, internal representations, attention/feature statistics, or training dynamics; they use offline, online/evolving, multi-teacher, or self-distillation schedules; and they often combine KD with complementary compression tools such as structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Effective distillation aligns the form and amount of transferred information with student capacity and task needs, and best practice is task-aware, hybrid, and selective about what to copy from the teacher.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Toolbox for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains the most flexible and broadly applicable approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Rather than a single recipe, KD is best treated as a toolbox: different distillation signals (logits, hidden states, attention/feature correlations), teacher schedules (offline, online/evolutionary, multi-teacher selection), and complementary techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, robustness objectives) should be chosen and combined according to task requirements, student capacity, data availability, and latency or robustness constraints. When KD is designed to align transferred information with student capacity and task needs it yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, NLP, generation, retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a broadly useful and adaptable family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP, KD methods extend beyond soft-target matching to include internal-representation transfer, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how it is transferred to student capacity, task properties, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods form a broad, task-aware toolbox for turning large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students. The literature spans soft-target (logit) matching, alignment of internal representations and attention, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical success typically requires adapting teacher signals to student capacity, selecting which signals to transfer given task constraints, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods when latency, data, or robustness requirements demand it.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring outputs, internal representations, and training dynamics from teacher models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label matching to a rich design space that includes intermediate-representation alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum- and route-based schedules, task-aware layer-wise filtering, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical and analytical work across vision and NLP shows that distillation, when matched to student capacity and task constraints and often combined with complementary compression methods, reliably improves compact-model performance while exposing remaining challenges in robustness, data requirements, and teacher–student mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task-Aware Hybrid Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware design space that can reliably compress large models into smaller, deployable students when its signals and schedules are matched to student capacity and task constraints. Combining soft-target transfer with representation-level alignment, teacher engineering (including multi- and online-teacher schemes and meta-learned teachers), adversarial/contrastive objectives, and hybrid pipelines that integrate pruning or progressive module replacement produces the strongest empirical trade-offs in latency, memory, and accuracy. Important caveats remain — notably teacher–student capacity gaps, data-complexity effects, and imperfect robustness transfer — which motivate careful choice of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Evolving, and Complementary to Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and versatile technique for compressing large deep models into compact students suitable for deployment. A broad and active literature has developed specialized KD variants that address teacher selection, internal representation transfer, robustness, task-specific filtering, online and ensemble distillation, and model-structure-aware compression. While KD is highly effective across vision and NLP tasks, recent work shows that pruning and module-replacement strategies can be competitive or complementary, particularly when unlabeled data or heavy distillation training is impractical. Best practice is to treat distillation as a toolbox: select methods that reduce teacher-student capacity gap, transfer internal representations and task-relevant features, and incorporate confidence or robustness objectives when needed, while considering pruning or progressive replacement when latency or data constraints dominate.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. The literature shows many complementary algorithmic families — soft-target (logit) transfer, internal-representation and attention/feature matching, contrastive and adversarial objectives, progressive module replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with structured pruning or module replacement. Empirical work across vision, NLP, summarization, retrieval, and reinforcement learning indicates that no single recipe dominates: careful matching of what is distilled to student capacity and task needs, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods tend to give the best accuracy–latency–size trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble models into smaller models to improve compact model quality and efficiency. Across vision, language, retrieval, and sequential decision-making, KD variants include soft-label distillation, internal-representation matching, layer-wise and module-replacement strategies, adversarial and contrastive formulations, multi-teacher and teacher-selection methods, online/evolutionary teacher schedules, and task-aware distillation that selects which teacher knowledge to transfer. KD has been combined with structured pruning and other compression approaches to achieve substantial speedups while preserving accuracy. Practical challenges include the teacher–student capacity gap, internal representation mismatch, the need for unlabeled data in some pipelines, and retaining robustness or previously learned knowledge in incremental settings. A range of remedies have been proposed: learning student-friendly or adaptive teachers, matching internal feature statistics, confidence-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware layer filters. In practice, distillation has enabled state-of-the-art trade-offs in NLP tasks (classification, summarization, retrieval, machine translation, and non-autoregressive generation), vision tasks, and reinforcement learning, while also being adapted for adversarial robustness and continual learning.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable, Task-Aware, Hybrid Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD has diversified beyond simple soft-label matching into a toolbox of methods—representation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schedules, curriculum- and route-based supervision, and hybrid pipelines that pair distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. When designed to match what is transferred to student capacity and the requirements of the target task, KD enables compact models that retain high accuracy, improved latency, and often better robustness than naïve compression approaches.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques provide a flexible design space for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students. Methods include soft-target (logit) matching, internal-representation alignment, layer- or module-wise replacement, multi- and online-teacher schedules, confidence- or curriculum-weighted supervision, and adversarial or contrastive objectives. Empirical results across vision and NLP show that combining representation-level transfer with teacher engineering and complementary compression (pruning or progressive replacement) typically yields the best trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and model size. Success depends on matching what is distilled to student capacity, adapting teacher signals to task constraints, and accounting for data complexity and robustness needs.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Effective distillation requires attention to what is transferred (logits, internal representations, feature maps, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are paired or trained (fixed teachers, learned teachers, multi-teacher or online schemes), and task-specific constraints. When combined with complementary approaches such as structured pruning or curriculum-style supervision, distillation yields compact models suitable for real-world NLP and vision deployments while enabling trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates information from large, high-capacity models into smaller, more efficient student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, and memory constraints. Over the past decade KD evolved from simple soft-target matching to a broad design space that includes internal-representation alignment, layer-wise and task-aware filtering, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical results across vision and NLP tasks (classification, retrieval, summarization, translation, and non-autoregressive generation) show that carefully selected or combined distillation strategies can substantially close the performance gap to teachers while delivering large reductions in size or latency. Practical success depends on matching what is transferred and how teachers and students are coupled to student capacity, task complexity, and data availability; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing which intermediate signals are task-relevant, and avoiding unnecessary constraints from overconfident or mismatched teachers.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce compact models that retain much of the performance of large networks by transferring knowledge from one or more teacher models to a student. Research over the last decade has diversified the KD toolkit beyond soft-label supervision to include internal representation matching, adversarial objectives, contrastive and Wasserstein distances, progressive module replacement, online and multi-teacher schemes, teacher-training strategies, and task-aware filter selection. These approaches have been applied across computer vision, NLP (including pretrained Transformers and summarization), retrieval, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Practical trade-offs arise from teacher-student capacity gaps, data requirements, optimization difficulties, and robustness concerns; contemporary work addresses these by narrowing capability gaps (e.g., evolving or student-friendly teachers), selecting or weighting teacher signals, and distilling only task-relevant intermediate features. Empirical studies show that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: the best choice depends on model architectures, target tasks, and constraints on data, latency, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques aim to transfer useful predictive behavior and internal structure from larger, expensive models to smaller, faster models. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, feature distributions, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are coupled (offline, online, multi-teacher, evolutionary, or self-distillation), and what additional objectives or defenses are used (adversarial training, contrastive losses, curriculum-based routing, or geodesic alignment). Distillation has been applied broadly across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and language understanding, and interacts with pruning and other compression strategies. Practical trade-offs include the teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness, and the form of supervision needed for good transfer.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Research converges on three core ideas: (1) the form of transferred information matters (from soft logits to internal representations and inter-feature statistics), (2) the teacher–student relationship and training schedule should be adapted to the student capacity and task, and (3) hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, curriculum or adversarial objectives, and task-aware filtering yield the best practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and robustness. Empirical work across machine translation, summarization, dense retrieval, non-autoregressive generation, vision, and 3D detection demonstrates large gains but also exposes sensitivity to data complexity, teacher selection, and capacity gaps, motivating ongoing research into targeted transfer mechanisms and efficient distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and NLP. The literature shows KD is not a single recipe but a design space of techniques (logits, internal representations, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules) that, when matched to student capacity and task demands and combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), yield strong trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and robustness. Effective practice requires selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals to the student, and hybridizing distillation with pruning or architecture-aware replacement where appropriate; remaining challenges include reliably transferring robustness, choosing task-relevant intermediate signals, and managing teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolkit for producing compact models in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD improves student performance by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, and training dynamics, but its success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, task demands, and deployment constraints. Best practice treats KD as part of a hybrid compression pipeline—selecting what to transfer, adapting teacher signals, and combining distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement when needed.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Flexible Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a core technique for compressing large models into efficient students for both vision and language tasks. A wide variety of KD formulations — from soft-label transfer and layer-wise matching to adversarial, online, and self-distillation — have demonstrated consistent gains in accuracy, inference speed, and memory footprint. However, distillation is not a single recipe: its effectiveness depends on teacher-student capacity gaps, the form of transferred information (logits, internal representations, attention maps), task characteristics, and data availability. Recent work shows that combining distillation with task-aware filtering, structured pruning, or teacher adaptation yields the best practical tradeoffs. Going forward, hybrid and task-aware distillation strategies that explicitly align representation, decision-boundary, and robustness objectives promise the most reliable compression outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Hybrid Toolbox for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a flexible, task-aware toolbox rather than a single algorithm. By selecting what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or structured behaviors), adapting teacher signals to student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, progressive module replacement, or teacher adaptation), practitioners can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and robustness constraints. Effective compression requires matching distillation strategies to task demands, data availability, and deployment constraints; blindly applying a single distillation recipe risks wasted effort or suboptimal trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple soft-label transfer into a broad, task-aware toolbox of methods for producing compact, deployable models. Contemporary KD techniques include matching logits, aligning internal representations or attention maps, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning or progressive module replacement. Empirical work across vision, language, and reinforcement learning shows that no single KD recipe dominates all settings: effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student capacity gaps, task complexity, and data availability. Practical compression typically requires selecting or adapting distilled signals to student capacity and combining complementary methods to meet latency, memory, and robustness constraints.
